articles.body:
A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell something at a predetermined price at a future date.

You don't usually need to pay the full value of the asset upfront. Instead, you deposit margin, which gives futures their powerful—and risky—leverage.

Simple example

Imagine S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) are trading at 6,500.

The ES contract multiplier is $50 × the index.

So:

Contract value = 6,500 × $50 = $325,000

You don't need $325,000 in cash to trade one contract. Your broker requires a much smaller amount of margin.

This creates leverage.

If ES moves:

6,500 → 6,510

That's a 10-point increase.

For one ES contract:

10 points × $50 = $500 profit 💰

If it falls 10 points instead:

10 points × $50 = $500 loss 🔴

Long vs. Short

It's very straightforward:

LONG futures 📈
You profit when the price rises and lose when it falls.

SHORT futures 📉
You profit when the price falls and lose when it rises.

Unlike stocks, futures markets are designed to make taking either side relatively straightforward.

What is margin?

Margin is not the purchase price of the futures contract.

Think of it more like collateral your broker requires to maintain the position.

For example:

Contract exposure: $325,000
Required margin: perhaps $20,000
Your exposure is still $325,000.

That's why futures can generate large gains or losses relative to the cash deposited.

⚠️ Your maximum loss is NOT limited to your margin deposit. Depending on the position and market movement, losses can exceed the initial amount you deposited.

Futures are marked to market

Profits and losses are calculated as the market moves and futures positions are marked to market daily.

If losses cause your account to fall below required margin levels, you may need additional funds or your broker may liquidate the position.

Why do futures exist?

There are two major reasons:

1. Hedging 🛡️

Businesses and investors use futures to reduce price risk.

An airline, for example, may want protection against rising fuel costs. A portfolio manager might use S&P 500 futures to reduce stock-market exposure.

2. Speculation 📊

Traders use futures to speculate on markets such as:

S&P 500 — ES
Nasdaq-100 — NQ
Crude Oil — CL
Gold — GC
Treasury bonds
Agricultural commodities
Currencies
Micro futures are useful to understand

There are smaller versions of popular index futures.

For example:

ES: $50 × S&P 500
MES: $5 × S&P 500

If the S&P 500 moves 10 points:

1 ES → $500

1 MES → $50

So MES provides 1/10th the exposure of ES, making position sizing easier for smaller accounts.

Futures vs. Stocks
	Stocks	Futures
Ownership	Own shares	Contract
Expiration	Usually none	Yes
Leverage	Usually lower	High
Short selling	More restrictions	Straightforward
Trading hours	Mostly market hours	Nearly 24 hours on many contracts
Margin	Optional depending on account	Core part of trading
Loss potential	Long stock limited to investment	Can exceed initial margin
The easiest way to remember it 🧠

Futures = Contract × Multiplier × Price

And your P&L is essentially:

Price movement × Contract multiplier × Number of contracts

So with MES, where the multiplier is $5:

+20 points × $5 × 2 contracts = +$200

But:

−20 points × $5 × 2 contracts = −$200

The multiplier and leverage are the two concepts you really want to understand before trading futures.
